issues.claim: In ASP.NET Core the distinction maps to two actions of an authentication scheme: challenge produces `401`, forbid produces `403`.
issues.problem: The statement is correct for bearer and JWT schemes, and the authorization middleware does call ChallengeAsync for unauthenticated users and ForbidAsync for authenticated users who fail a policy. For the cookie scheme, challenge and forbid redirect (302) to the login and access-denied pages instead of returning 401 and 403. No cited link or excerpt covers this ASP.NET Core claim.
issues.suggestedFix: Qualify it in both locales: "for API (bearer/JWT) schemes challenge produces 401 and forbid produces 403 (the cookie scheme redirects instead)". Optionally add the ASP.NET Core authorization docs as a link, with matching linkTitles in both locales.

issues.claim: Find the line where HttpClient reads the response body without checking the status code
issues.problem: The title (and its RU counterpart) names the defect and effectively points at line 7, which weakens the find-bug exercise. The guide's own example title is more neutral.
issues.suggestedFix: Use a neutral title such as "Find the line that makes the program crash on a 404 response", and in RU "Найдите строку, из-за которой программа падает при ответе 404".

issues.claim: It throws `HttpRequestException` only when the request itself fails, for example on a connection or DNS error
issues.problem: Slightly incomplete: a timeout or cancellation surfaces as TaskCanceledException, not HttpRequestException. Not misleading for this question.
issues.suggestedFix: Optionally write "throws only when the request itself fails (connection or DNS error, timeout or cancellation) and never because of the status code", and mirror it in RU.
